stories.summary: We have your one-stop shop for everything you need to keep up with all the action this October.
stories.body:
The 2026 MLB playoffs are in full swing!

The 12-team postseason began with an action-packed wild-card round that featured eight teams battling for four spots to advance to the eight-team division series.

The Chicago White Sox became the first team to win a series this postseason with a wild-card round sweep of the Houston Astros. Then the New York Yankees swept the Boston Red Sox in two routs, recording the highest series run differential in the history of the current wild-card format. The San Diego Padres also sealed their spot in the NLDS with a sweep of the Chicago Cubs. In the only wild-card series to go the distance, the Atlanta Braves held off the Philadelphia Phillies to move on.

The Los Angeles Dodgers beat the Braves to nab the first spot in the championship series, where they are facing the Milwaukee Brewers after they beat the Padres.

The Tampa Bay Rays swept the Yankees to clinch the first spot in the ALCS and face the Cleveland Guardians, who mounted a stunning comeback against the White Sox after dropping the first two games of the ALDS.

From the first pitch of the wild-card games to the last out of the World Series, we've got you covered with the postseason bracket, schedules, results and how to watch every game this October.

stories.headline: Andy Burnham: Man City owners didn't mention Premier League charges in meeting
stories.summary: Andy Burnham has said Manchester City's owners and directors did not raise the Premier League's charges against the club when he met with them.
stories.body:
Andy Burnham has said Manchester City's owners and directors did not raise the Premier League's charges against the club when he met with them.

The Prime Minister said he was "very happy" to set out details of the meetings, after they were published on Monday.

Manchester City have been found guilty on all counts of breaching the Premier League's financial rules and "the majority of charges" relating to failing to co-operate with the league's investigation.

On Monday it was revealed Burnham had a formal meeting with Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak at an investment summit, chatted to him in the stands at former City captain Vincent Kompany's testimonial and was accompanied by staff from the club on official overseas visits.

- Man City 'deserved' trophies - PSG boss Luis Enrique on charges

- Football Regulator chair will quit if politics interferes with any Man City investigation

Burnham was asked about the meetings during Prime Minister's Questions by Conservative MP Jerome Mayhew (Broadland and Fakenham).

Mayhew said: "The Prime Minister sees himself as a man of candour.

"So will he tell the House, did anyone associated with the running of Manchester City Football Club raise the charges they were facing, and have now been found guilty of, either with him or any member of his team?"

Burnham said: "They did not raise those issues with me.

"I'm very happy, Mr Speaker, for everything to be set out in full.

"It is why I asked the Greater Manchester Combined Authority [GMCA], in response to a call from the Leader of the Opposition and others, to set out a full statement of my key dealings with the owners of Manchester City Football Club.

"That statement was published on Monday, and it includes the issues in the news today.

"That is the position."

Details of the Prime Minister's contacts with the scandal-hit club and its Abu Dhabi owners during his time as Greater Manchester mayor were released by the combined authority earlier this week.

Burnham had told MPs that "all of my dealings" with Manchester City's owners would be published.

A GMCA spokesman said: "In October 2021 Andy Burnham, in his role as mayor of Greater Manchester, had a formal meeting with Khaldoon Al Mubarak at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit arranged by the Department for International Trade.

"In his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions, including attending Vincent Kompany's testimonial match in September 2019, where he met the chairman informally in the stands.

"These have been declared in the usual way.

"Also during his time as mayor, representatives of Greater Manchester sporting clubs would routinely join business delegations as part of mayoral international visits.

"This included representatives from Manchester United travelling to Austin and Dublin, Lancashire Cricket Club joining a delegation to India, and Manchester City staff supporting visits to China and Japan."

stories.headline: Lamine Yamal: Assist for Anthony Gordon in Barcelona win 'almost-rabona'
stories.summary: Lamine Yamal christened his dribble leading to Anthony Gordon's goal against Galatasaray an "almost-rabona" as Barcelona ran out 4-1 winners in the Champions League game.
stories.body:
Lamine Yamal christened his dribble leading to Anthony Gordon's goal against Galatasaray an "almost-rabona" as Barcelona ran out 4-1 winners in the Champions League game.

Yamal, 19, didn't score in the victory in Istanbul but produced a stunning second half display, setting up Fermín López with a pinpoint cross before creating for Gordon.

The teenager shaped to do a rabona, tricking the defender, only to knock the ball towards the byline instead. He benefitted from a small ricochet, but reacted quickly to drive inside before assisting the England international.

"I don't know what to call it, it was an almost-rabona dribble," Yamal told Movistar after the game as he watched a replay of the goal.

"It came off well to set up Gordon, that's the main thing, that it was effective at the end of the day."

In a separate interview with CBS, Yamal told former Barça forward Thierry Henry he is always looking for new ways to create space.

"Recently, I have noticed that a lot of opponents, whenever I reach the byline, go to ground, so I saw the opportunity, went for it and it came off," he added.

"I always try to faint to create space. If you can create a bit of space that way, it gives us [attackers] life. It was nice, but also effective, so I am very happy."

- Flick urges caution as Barcelona extend perfect start with Champions League win

- Champions League recap: Atleti beat Man United, Viking snatch point vs. Bayern

- Transfer rumors, news: Real Madrid, Barcelona chase Spurs defender Porro

In 10 appearances for Barça this season, Yamal has now scored eight goals and laid on nine assists.

Barça coach Hansi Flick credited him with "changing the game" against Galatasaray as the Spanish champions recovered from going behind to run out convincing winners.

"In the second half he was fantastic, how he dominated the game, the last pass ... It's unbelievable what he's doing," Flick said in the post game news conference.

The victory in Türkiye was Barça's 10th in a row at the start of the current campaign -- eight in LaLiga and two in the Champions League.

During that time, they have netted a remarkable 43 goals, with Yamal saying they are laying the foundations for potentially historic season.

"Always," he told CBS when asked if Barça believe a Treble -- winning LaLiga, the Champions League and the Copa del Rey -- is possible this season.

"We're Barcelona, we're the best team in the world."

That claim will be tested over the next week as Barça travel to third-placed Real Betis in LaLiga on Saturday, face Paris Saint-Germain in France in the Champions League next Tuesday and then host Real Madrid in the first Clásico of the season the following Sunday.

stories.headline: Fantasy football matchup rankings: Upgrade Tony Pollard, fade Trevor Lawrence
stories.summary: The most and least favorable matchups in the NFL for this week's games at the four key fantasy positions.
stories.body:
Making tough lineup decisions each week can be the most challenging part of fantasy football. When you're torn between two similar players, start the player with the superior matchup.

But exactly how does one determine the best (and worst) weekly matchups?

The matchup rankings provide a schedule-independent method to evaluate positional matchups, ranking all 32 opposing defenses in order of most to least favorable for opposing players at all four skill positions. Instead of relying upon seasonal totals, we calibrate points-allowed data to show how each defense fared relative to the difficulty of the schedule it has faced over the past five weeks. This provides a fairer approach to judging the quality of individual matchups.

"Adj. FPA," or Adjusted Fantasy Points Allowed, reflects how far above or below players' weekly PPR fantasy point averages that defense held opponents at that position. A positive number means that the matchup is favorable; a negative number means it is unfavorable. Additionally, remember teams often use multiple running backs and wide receivers in a game, and these plus/minus averages cover all of a team's personnel at that position.

Finally, a caveat: Matchups are only one ingredient in my rankings formula. Not every favorable matchup should be exploited, nor unfavorable matchup avoided. If you want the most complete source for whom to start, consult our weekly rankings.

Quarterbacks

Matchups highlight: Kirk Cousins, Las Vegas Raiders (versus Buffalo Bills). Two of the top 10 quarterbacks in fantasy points per game are on bye in Week 6 (QB3 Jared Goff, QB8 Joe Burrow), and another two aren't guarantees to play (QB5 Caleb Williams, QB9 Lamar Jackson), so this is a week where some creativity might be required to fill the position. Cousins, QB11 on the list, and the ninth-best quarterback in terms of passer rating, is a worthwhile streamer, thanks in large part to his matchup. The Bills have allowed three 25-plus-point fantasy scores to opposing quarterbacks, matching the Detroit Lions and Washington Commanders for most in the league, as well as the second-most pass completions per game (26.8). Bills-Raiders also has the week's highest over/under (53.5), with the Raiders giving 5.5 points, signaling that another pass-friendly game script should be in order.

Others to like:

Brock Purdy, San Francisco 49ers (versus Commanders, Monday night)

Jordan Love, Green Bay Packers (versus Dallas Cowboys, Sunday night)

Matchup to avoid: Trevor Lawrence, Jacksonville Jaguars (versus Houston Texans in London, Sunday 9:30 a.m. ET). His performance in London over the weekend wasn't as impressive as his final fantasy score indicated (21.74 points); bear in mind that 43% of his production came with his team trailing in the fourth quarter. Lawrence has had a fine year from an on-field standpoint, but his fantasy results have been hit-or-miss. Facing a defense with the amount of talent the Texans have -- at least on paper -- he's one of the shakiest Week 6 starters. Lawrence has a horrendous career history against his division rival; he has averaged 11.6 fantasy points in 10 career starts against the Texans and 8.2 against them in four meetings from 2024 to 2025.

Running backs

Matchups highlight: Tony Pollard, Tennessee Titans (at Indianapolis Colts). If there's any week to trust Pollard as a clear fantasy RB2, it's one in which three top-20 running backs in terms of fantasy points per game (RB1 Jahmyr Gibbs, RB17 Aaron Jones Sr., RB18 Chase Brown) are on bye and where he gets to face one of the league's struggling run defenses. The Colts just got pummeled for 36.8 fantasy points by Jaylen Warren in Week 5, meaning they've surrendered two of the position's five best single-game scores this season. They've also allowed the fourth-most points per rushing attempt and the third-most points per target to running backs, giving Pollard multiple potential avenues to success.

Others to like:

Rhamondre Stevenson, New England Patriots (versus New York Jets)

Cam Skattebo, New York Giants (versus New Orleans Saints)

MarShawn Lloyd, Packers (versus Cowboys)

Matchup to avoid: Quinshon Judkins, Cleveland Browns (versus Baltimore Ravens). He's getting enough play to generally warrant fantasy RB2 status, with 61% snap and 58% rushing shares that rank 17th and 14th at the position, respectively, but his results have been lackluster, to say the least. Among running backs with at least 30 carries, his 3.0 yards per carry and 4.1% explosive rates are both third worst, and he has a 19% stuff rate, per Next Gen Stats. That bodes poorly for Judkins in a matchup against the Ravens, the fourth-best defense in terms of Adjusted Fantasy Points Allowed, as well as the sixth best in terms of run stop rate against running backs (29.0%).

Wide receivers

Matchups highlight: Christian Watson/Matthew Golden, Packers (versus Cowboys). Jordan Love's passing was simply magical in Week 5 against the Chicago Bears, as he amassed 256 yards on deep throws (20-plus yards downfield), the third most by any player in the 20 years for which the data has been tracked. The matchup had a lot to do with it, as the Bears rank 31st in passer rating allowed in those situations. The Cowboys aren't much better, ranking 28th. The Cowboys have seen an opposing wide receiver score in excess of 15 fantasy points in each of the past four weeks, so they're as good a matchup for these two wideouts to challenge for a top-10 positional point total as last week's was.

Others to like:

Mike Evans, 49ers (versus Commanders, MNF)

Tre Tucker, Raiders (versus Bills)

Jalen Coker, Carolina Panthers (at Philadelphia Eagles)

Matchup to avoid: Michael Wilson, Arizona Cardinals (at Los Angeles Rams). The Marvin Harrison Jr. trade didn't seem to change much with Wilson's role, as he went from 96% route participation and a 29% target share in the first four games to 85% and 15% in Week 5, as Kendrick Bourne and Jalen Brooks also played meaningful roles. Wilson remains Jacoby Brissett's preferred wide receiver when throwing, but with tight end Trey McBride serving the Cardinals' true "WR1" role, Wilson will remain subject to his matchups. This is a poor one, largely due to the stellar play of Rams CB Trent McDuffie, who has contributed to the Rams having a league-leading minus-5.6 Adj. FPA against opposing WR1s.

Tight ends

Matchups highlight: Dallas Goedert, Eagles (versus Panthers). In his return to action following a knee injury, Goedert managed a 24% target share and 9.8 fantasy points despite a challenging matchup against the Jaguars in London, stepping up as a safety net for Jalen Hurts while his No. 1 wide receiver, DeVonta Smith (hamstring), remained sidelined. We'll see whether Smith is able return for Week 6, but even if he can, Goedert's matchup is significantly more favorable this week and likely to keep him within the position's top 10. The opposing Panthers have seen three different tight ends post season highs in fantasy points against them: Cole Kmet (11.5, Week 1), Harold Fannin Jr. (24.1, Week 3) and Sam LaPorta (22.4, Week 4).

Matchup to avoid: Brenton Strange, Jaguars (versus Texans). He's quietly putting together a productive fantasy season, ranking 13th among tight ends in fantasy points per game (10.1), largely because he has the position's 10th-largest target share (19%) and fourth-best catch rate (81%). That keeps him barely beneath the fantasy TE1 cutoff most weeks, but a Texans matchup is limiting to his upside. The Texans have struggled much more against wide receivers (6.5 Adj. FPA) than tight ends (minus-3.2 Adj. FPA) and have afforded the position a single target in the red zone so far.

stories.headline: First-round Phantom Draft: An early look at who goes where, when bids will come
stories.summary: The AFL trade period is over and attention turns to the draft. So who goes where? When will bids land? Here's Jasper Chellappah's early, first-round Phantom Draft.
stories.body:
It's finally draft season.

Changes to draft points and matching bids make for complications on the four club-tied prospects in this Phantom Draft, but they also shorten the first round to 18 selections.

It's a hotly-contested race to be the first overall pick in the open draft. Midfielder Ethan Drever and goalkicker Arki Butler have inside track to be that choice for Essendon, but the decision is still to be narrowed down with Heath Mellody, Harry Van Hattum, and Gus Teixeira all making strong cases.

Bidding changes mean clubs may only match with two selections, and a 20% points loading is given to the Brisbane Lions for making the Grand Final whereas Port Adelaide and GWS receive a 10% discount for missing finals.

It means picks are absorbed within the first round to effectively shorten night one of the AFL Draft.

Recruiters love the depth of the crop that has emerged this year, but a real evenness in talent from 15 through 30 will make for volatile slides and rises come November.

Exactly five weeks out from the 2026 AFL Draft, this is ESPN's first-round Phantom Draft.

1. BID - Port Adelaide: Dougie Cochrane

Port Adelaide/South Australia

FWD/MID/DEF, 195cm

Essendon has all but guaranteed Port Adelaide it will be bidding on Cochrane first overall. He's worth the hype; a roaming key forward with midfield ambitions that played the final month of an injury-plagued top-age campaign behind the ball as a designated kicker. Cochrane has been the nominal first choice in this draft for 24 months and Port Adelaide will have no issue matching, and they've left the door open for clubs to come calling for picks seven and 12 in the lead-up to draft night.

Picks used: 7 and 12

2. Essendon: Ethan Drever

GWV Rebels/Vic Country

MID, 188cm

It's still far from a guarantee that Essendon opt for Drever but there's growing buzz around the powerful midfielder. An injury-free season set him up to dominate for club and state alike, with the Ballarat local producing gaudy numbers for the Rebels and Vic Country. He runs hard both ways, uses his legs to drive out of contest and has a penchant for kicking long-running goals. Similarly to 2016 when they selected skipper Andrew McGrath, the Dons don't have a clear no. 1 in the open pool.

In the mix: Arki Butler, Heath Mellody

3. Richmond: Arki Butler

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

MID/FWD, 182cm

Richmond's decision here will be highly dependent on their intel into West Coast and Melbourne after them. Butler presents as the best on the board and most unlikely to be available at their next selection. He's a match-winner inside forward 50 with aerial strength and tricks at ground level, kicking goals in bunches and pinch-hitting with power through the middle. With a host of tall forwards and midfielders drafted in recent years, Butler fits nicely amongst the young Tigers nucleus but real interest in Harry Van Hattum could see them flip this order.

In the mix: Harry Van Hattum, Ethan Drever

4. BID - Carlton: Cody Walker

Carlton VFL/Vic Country

MID, 184cm

The Blues are banking on a Walker bid arriving after pick two. Picks 13 and 18 (which become 12 and 17 after a Cochrane bid) is enough to match a bid from three onwards with a minor points deficit. If Essendon surprises by reading out Walker's name in the first two the Blues must have contingencies in place so the son-of-a-gun doesn't slip through. Walker is worthy of a bid at two - he plays at breakneck speed with elite acceleration and evasiveness through the midfield, impressing week in, week out for Carlton's VFL side.

The son of Andrew opted to nominate the Blues over academy club Richmond this year which may dissuade the Tigers from making a bid, but this is close to the end of Walker's draft range and West Coast already has history bidding on Blues father-sons.

Picks used: 12 and 17

5. West Coast: Heath Mellody

Claremont/Western Australia

MID/DEF, 184cm

The hometown kid enjoyed the strongest finish to 2026 of any prospect. Mellody claimed the Larke Medal at the national championships, made his WAFL debut and was one of Claremont's best performers up to the grand final. His name sits comfortably amongst the best in the class with his work rate, clean hands and class by foot making him the perfect complement to Harley Reid and Willem Duursma.

In the mix: Arki Butler, Gus Teixeira

6. Melbourne (via Port Adelaide): Mitch Harris

Woodville-West Torrens/South Australia

DEF, 195cm

Melbourne made a deal to move up two spots in the draft, effectively jumping North's selection at the time. That pick now lands with Sydney but it shouldn't impact who the Dees had in mind. Harris is the bolter this year, rising from a likely second round prospect at the start of the season to the consensus best key defender in the pool. He locks down, intercepts and has shown flashes up forward, plus impressed in SANFL finals to finish the season against mature bodies. The Swans will have interest in Harris given their shallow key defensive stocks, but the Dees will kick off his draft range at this point.

In the mix: Harry Van Hattum, Heath Mellody

7. Richmond (via Port Adelaide): Harry Van Hattum

Northern Knights/Vic Metro

RUC/FWD, 205cm

Richmond would be thrilled to see Van Hattum get through to the pick they brought in via Port Adelaide. The big ruck trained with the club over pre-season and he ripped games apart at various stages of 2026. Van Hattum plays with a physical edge, follows up as an extra midfielder and uses the ball beautifully off his favoured right boot. He looms as the perfect replacement for skipper Toby Nankervis, so much so that Van Hattum could even be snapped up by the Tigers with their first selection before Melbourne gets a look in.

In the mix: Gus Teixeira, Mitch Harris

8. BID - GWS: Ethan Matthews

GWS made an early bid on Harry Kyle last year and Sydney can return the favour here. Trading into pick six via the Blakey deal puts the Swans firmly in the range of Matthews, an excellent midfield prospect that racks up the ball and uses it with composure off his left foot. GWS would be matching with pick 11 at this stage, and could look to trade points into future years on the night to maximise their draft hand while still landing their academy gun. Matthews is clearly the best Giants Academy prospect since Tom Green in 2019.

Picks used: 11 and 19

9. Sydney (via North Melbourne): Gus Teixeira

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

MID, 181cm

If the top key defender is off the board the Swans will have an eye on the best available talent, having not drafted a top-10 talent since Logan McDonald and Braeden Campbell in 2020. Teixeira is the highly rated prospect that slides in this phantom, but could easily be snapped up by the Dees or Tigers prior. Playing with powerful drive in the forward half, Teixeira's impact with ball in hand has been a standout all season. He'll start his career as a general forward but there's little doubt amongst recruiters that Teixeira will soon be a midfielder at the next level.

In the mix: Mitch Harris, Tyson Bradley

10. Gold Coast (FA compensation): Sam Gayfer

Northern Knights/Vic Metro

FWD, 194cm

Gayfer is deserving of a top 10 pick this year and the Suns come into this selection through Ben King's departure. Even while bringing in Aidan Schubert their key forward stocks are thin and Gayfer is the competitive beast that Damien Hardwick covets. He crashes packs, pressures at ground level and can jump on heads to take massive marks. The Suns swooping here would be a blow for the Saints and Pies who are keen on the athletic tall.

In the mix: Tyson Bradley, Clancy Snell

11. BID - Brisbane: Caylen Murray

Lions Academy/Allies

DEF/MID, 183cm

The Keidean Coleman trade to Essendon at the death gives Brisbane three picks in the second round that will need to be consolidated to match a bid at this stage. The academy star has some similarities to Coleman in his precise ball use off halfback. He generates run and is safe with ball in hand, making the right decisions and creating space for himself and others. Murray appeals as a replacement for Dayne Zorko and could play significant football in 2027, with the Saints on the lookout for a ball user of his quality.

12. St Kilda: Wil Malady

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

FWD, 190cm

The Saints would love to see Gayfer here as a key forward option, but have a nice group of talls to pick from. Malady is the wildcard play, with excellent athleticism including a big leap and sensational agility at his size. He works himself into the ground as a link between the forwards and midfielders, but can also play deep as a dangerous aerial target.

In the mix: Sam Gayfer, Lochie Burrows

13. Collingwood: Tyson Bradley

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

DEF, 195cm

The Pies are in the market for a tall at either end of the ground and will get one at this spot. Bradley is ultra composed and a steady kick out of defence, twisting and turning out of trouble and relieving pressure for his side. He also competes well in the air against key forwards including successful matchups on Malady and Gayfer in finals contests. Clubs have loved his leadership and character qualities so he could land even higher than this mark. Collingwood will be eager to see if Gayfer gets through as the nephew of premiership defender Mick.

In the mix: Sam Gayfer, Clancy Snell, Wil Malady

14. Melbourne (via Port Adelaide): Leo Steed

Swan Districts/Western Australia

MID, 176cm

If the Dees go tall with Harris or Van Hattum first they can get their midfielder here. Steed is ultra professional, a two-way runner and brings his courage and toughness to every contest. Recruiters are confident the WA hard nut makes it as an on-baller at the next level and Melbourne is primed to add youth to that area of the ground.

In the mix: Toby Krasna, Jake Eime

15. Adelaide: Clancy Snell

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

DEF, 196cm

The Crows held onto Nick Murray but lost Jordon Butts and are thin down back. Snell gives them a high-upside swing at the best intercept defender in the class. He's an elite aerialist that backs himself to kickstart transition. They remain in need of some dash out of defence with local product Jake Eime's range beginning at this point too.

In the mix: Tyson Bradley, Jake Eime, Kodah Edwards

16. St Kilda (via Geelong): Lochie Burrows

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

DEF/MID, 181cm

The Saints are keen on Burrows. A local Bentleigh product whose best trait may be his versatility, Burrows has been thrown around the ground and excelled everywhere. He can get his hands dirty as a contested midfielder, lock down and offer dash out of defence and worked hard on his forward craft over pre-season with an eye to a role off half forward. If the Saints sniff out interest in Burrows around this mark they could even snap up the high-character talent with their first selection.

In the mix: Leo Steed, Jackson Phillips, Jake Eime

17. Essendon (via Hawthorn): George Dimer

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

FWD, 173cm

Dimer earns big plaudits from clubs for his character and selfless nature. As a small forward he has the speed to separate and the nous to sniff out the goals but also plays with a team-first attitude that sees him set up a lot of scores. He played midfield in his juniors and brings his ball-winning to the forward half. Small forward is a huge area of need for the Dons but there will also be a host of clubs keen on Dimer from this stage on.

In the mix: Clancy Snell, Jack Pickett, Toby Krasna

18. Fremantle: Jake Soutar

East Perth

DEF, 190cm

The Dockers are entrenched in their premiership window and Soutar would have played significant football at a lot of clubs towards the end of 2026. The 20-year-old was East Perth's fairest and best after a breakout season in the WAFL, intercepting and creating off halfback including a big finals campaign. He's a good size to play on various forwards and has the body to compete for Luke Ryan's role straight away. A mature-ager is a bold selection in the first round but Soutar is a win-now pick in a role Fremantle needs to address.

In the mix: Leo Steed, Toby Krasna

stories.headline: Wemby, Spurs have 'clarity' after Finals loss but know "nothing is guaranteed'
stories.summary: The Spurs enter the season with expectations to return to the Finals after loss to the Knicks.
stories.body:
IT'S A MUGGY Sunday in September at Frost Bank Center, and San Antonio Spurs media day is still a little more than two weeks away.

As the sun peeks through the arena's east entrance, condensation trickles down the floor-to-ceiling windows, a testament to the 86% humidity outside and similar to the pressure cooker inside the building for fans vying for a spot on Victor Wembanyama's official handpicked Spurs supporters group: the Jackals.

"This is something that hasn't been done to this level," said Aidan Sterling, president of the Jackals. "All the people who weren't Jackals last year, all the new guys, I know there's nerves amongst them."

Jitters would set in for some of the returning Jackals, too. Because unless they earned designation as "pack leader," membership isn't guaranteed this season, just like the Spurs aren't assured a spot in the 2026-27 NBA Finals after last season's shocking run that ended a six-year postseason drought and captivated fans.

"There's a lot of competition," said one of the Jackals' pack leaders. "Being a part of it last season doesn't guarantee you a spot this year."

It's a reality the Spurs understand all too well when measuring prospects for the upcoming season against the gauntlet that is the NBA's Western Conference, not to mention a vastly improved East or the fact that no team has advanced to the Finals in consecutive seasons since the 2018-19 Golden State Warriors. It's why Wembanyama and the rest of the squad tread carefully when discussing the sky-high expectations thrust upon the club in the wake of a 28-win improvement and Finals appearance. Wembanyama turned heads going into last season when revealing the team's goal of advancing to the postseason as a top-six seed.

Then, at September's media day, Wembanyama mentioned, "I couldn't imagine better motivation" coming off a 4-1 series loss to the New York Knicks in the NBA Finals. The 22-year-old was the only Spur that day to openly discuss specifics regarding expectations for the upcoming season.

"We have some goals between us that we're going to keep between us as teammates," Wembanyama said. "We won the West last year. We don't want to do anything less this year. We want to be the first seed, and then we want to keep fighting for this top spot."

To do that, San Antonio plans to lean on process to spin success the way it has done for decades. It's the approach the Spurs used last season, focusing on internal improvement and the day-to-day to help them manage an 82-game regular season and an extended postseason.

In their minds, that's the only way to return to the game's grandest stage.

It's a methodology dating to former coach Gregg Popovich's 29-season tenure in which San Antonio established a South Texas dynasty that churned out five titles and a record-tying run of 22 consecutive playoff appearances.

At Pop's final media day as head coach during Wembanyama's second season, the Hall of Famer explained that, "even when we were a championship-caliber team, we never said we're going to win this many games. It was never a point of discussion."

It still isn't, even with a new regime calling the shots.

"Our expectation is to continue to try to improve and be the best version of this team we can be," Spurs coach Mitch Johnson said. "The expectations are kind of like big games, right? There's added enthusiasm, excitement, criticism, opinion. I've been on both sides of it now in this league, and I'll take the expectations."

AS PANDEMONIUM ERUPTED on the Frost Bank Center floor when the Knicks celebrated their first championship in 53 years, Wembanyama stoically scratched at the back of his head at a lectern just a few feet away, perplexed by how San Antonio fell short in a Finals series in which the Spurs held double-digit leads in every game.

"[All] five games this series had the same scenario," Wembanyama said. "[It was surprising] how relentless we were in our mistakes, and [how] they were in punishing them."

In the days that followed their loss, Wembanyama, his teammates and the coaching staff set upon the task of finding out why as they headed into the summer. Yet no one is willing to divulge exactly what they learned went awry in the Finals.

"We have a lot of clarity on why we feel like we lost and what we can do to get better," said Spurs guard Stephon Castle, who is one-third of the Spurs' expected starting backcourt.

Castle, De'Aaron Fox and rising second-year guard Dylan Harper, who shined against the Knicks in the Finals as a sixth man, played just 69 minutes together last season, including 25 in the Finals, and were outscored by 47 points in those minutes, according to ESPN Research. By comparison, the Spurs had a plus-9.4 net rating when Fox and Castle shared the floor in the regular season, plus-6.2 with Fox and Harper, and plus-11.0 with Harper and Castle. Internally, the Spurs have faith in the three-guard construction, believing Castle and Harper possess the size to consistently hold their own against wings. All three threaten opponents as penetrators able to drive into the paint at will.

"We're very fortunate to have such a dynamic roster where you can really get creative in terms of puzzle pieces and how you want to build out the puzzle," Johnson said. "We saw it at times with the three guards in addition to what you can do around Victor. ... There's definite growth for those three guys just in terms of playing off each other and continuing to complement each other."

New lead assistant Billy Donovan, who replaced Sean Sweeney when he took the head coaching job in Orlando, will be charged with fostering the on-court growth of the three guards when they're on the floor together. During the few brief portions of practice open to media, Donovan was working with Fox, Castle and Harper on the floor at the same time.

"It's been great," Fox said. "One thing we've talked about is him being able to coach three guards at the same time. When he was [head coach] in OKC, he had Dennis [Schroder], Shai [Gilgeous-Alexander] and [Chris Paul]. So, he's been able to make it work. That team wasn't supposed to go to the playoffs at the time and then ended up playing well because they figured it out. That's one thing he's bringing to us."

WEMBANYAMA WASTED NO time jumping back in the lab after San Antonio's Finals loss and looked to make the most of the shortest offseason of his young career. In addition to working with Hall of Famer Hakeem Olajuwon for the second consecutive summer, Wembanyama and several Spurs, including free agent addition Tobias Harris, visited Fox for workouts at his home gym outside Houston.

"We had a long season, but you don't want to go the entire summer without being able to be around your teammates and getting in the gym together," Fox said. "Just being able to be around each other, I think, is big. We have a group of guys that like being around each other."

Wembanyama tested that notion in August by inviting several teammates to Paris for more work on the court, in addition to sightseeing and fellowship. Wembanyama wanted his teammates to know where he came from to get to where he is now as a generational superstar.

So, the reigning Defensive Player of the Year and his teammates worked out at Palais des Sports Maurice Thorez, where Wembanyama's professional basketball career began as a gangly teenager with Nanterre 92. Wembanyama described the time with his teammates as touching, emotional even.

"They were willing to make this trip, and they were also curious about what I wanted to show them," Wembanyama said. "So it matters because these people matter to me. This place matters to me. Having the two of them together is kind of the same as when family comes to visit here."

Second-year forward Carter Bryant sat with Wembanyama on plane rides as a rookie last season, discussing "our personal goals, team goals, collective goals [and] off-the-court goals." He said he enjoyed the fellowship in France with his teammate, coming away impressed by how far Wembanyama has come, and how he has maintained humility, which has helped him to grow as a leader.

"[It was big] for us to take the time out of our summers after we had been together longer than anybody, then come to his home and for him to educate us about where he's from, [to] just be around him in his element," Bryant said. "For him to get to that point and come back to where he started and then have the people around him that are like, 'Yo, next year we're going to take that next step.' Not too many people get that experience."

In between the work on the court and deep conversations about what took place during the Finals, the Spurs in Paris broke bread together on multiple occasions, including one dinner on a riverboat on the Seine River with the Eiffel Tower as the backdrop. During the visit to Paris, Bryant and his girlfriend biked 32 miles one day. Veteran forward Harrison Barnes even set up a tour of the Louvre for the visiting Spurs.

Wembanyama continued his summer work while his teammates visited Paris by taking Barnes with him to train with a French rugby club. There, the 7-foot-4 center said he worked to improve his balance.

So, even after a season in which Wembanyama became the NBA's youngest and first unanimous Defensive Player of the Year, finished third in MVP voting and led San Antonio to the Finals for the first time in 12 seasons, Bryant couldn't help but marvel at Wembanyama's insistence on involving his teammates in his offseason work.

"With a franchise like this, the biggest thing is family having each other's backs and understanding what we stand for as a unit," Bryant said.

SAN ANTONIO UNDERSTANDS the challenge ahead of returning to the Finals. Even if the Spurs consistently play at their peak, forces beyond their control could derail everything.

Injuries and the matchup against the upstart Spurs stopped the Oklahoma City Thunder last season from returning to the Finals. The Indiana Pacers' bid for a return ended before the next season even began with Tyrese Haliburton tearing his right Achilles tendon in Game 7 of that series against OKC. Injuries also slammed the brakes on the 2024-25 Boston Celtics' potential return to the Finals, while the 2024-25 Dallas Mavericks vanquished their prospects by trading away their best player, Luka Doncic.

The last team to win the title after losing in the Finals the previous year was the Warriors, who used a once-in-a-generation cap spike to add Kevin Durant to a core that had already won a title in 2015. The Spurs' only notable free agent signing was Harris, a 15-year veteran who has never been beyond the second round of the playoffs.

Still, the Spurs know they can't just jump straight back to the Finals to make up for the mistakes that cost them the series against the Knicks. Throughout the entire organization, everyone has bought in to the idea of taking everything one step at a time -- the same approach they used last season.

"It's human nature, right," Spurs forward Devin Vassell said. "You want to be back in that situation, but you can't skip a day. You can't skip training camp. You can't skip the preseason. You can't skip opening night. You can't skip the lone back-to-backs. You can't sit here and snap your fingers [and] you're back in the Finals. It just doesn't work like that. Nothing is guaranteed. So, we've got to keep implementing what we were doing last year, stuff that carried over and just building good habits. We can't fast forward anything. So, just take it day by day."

Veterans Barnes and Luke Kornet advanced to the NBA Finals at previous stops. Golden State captured a title in Barnes' first Finals appearance (2015) but fell the next season 4-3 to the Cleveland Cavaliers.

Kornet, meanwhile, played for the Celtics in the 2022 Finals, which the Warriors won in six games, and returned in 2024, when the Celtics beat the Mavericks in five games to end a sixteen-year title drought, three years longer than San Antonio's current titleless run.

"For us, it's a matter of focus that we have every single day in terms of what's our standard we're setting for ourselves and comparing it against that," Barnes explained. "I don't think it's one of those things where you simply carry momentum from one season to the next. You have to come back and start the journey from day one again.

"I do think there's something that sharpens your focus, like shared heartbreak. And mind you, health is always a major factor. Those things are out of your control. But for the things that are in your control, having that experience helps you frame how you approach every single day."

Several fans at the Jackals' tryouts could relate, showing their dedication in front of Sterling in a Chewbacca costume underneath a David Robinson jersey, and, of course, green alien garb.

Meanwhile, San Antonio's alien, Wembanyama, and his teammates continue to temper expectations for the season.

"This isn't pressure," Sterling said. "This is passion."

stories.summary: With just two contests on the NHL calendar Wednesday, here are game previews, betting lines, updated stat leaders and more.
stories.body:
After the hockey overload of Frozen Frenzy on Tuesday -- with all 32 teams in action -- Wednesday's schedule is a much lighter dessert, although both matchups are quite tantalizing.

The early game features the returning Eastern Conference finalist Canadiens against the Capitals, who hope to have a long playoff run in Alex Ovechkin's final NHL season. In the second game, two Western Conference juggernauts -- the Stars and the Avalanche -- hold a rematch just 24 hours after battling during the Frenzy.

7:30 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | WSH -130, O/U: 6.5

After being anointed as the next big thing during the preseason, the Canadiens have stumbled out of the starting blocks, posting a 3-2-1 record. Likewise, the Capitals were declared the unofficial winners of the offseason given their many wise trade and free agency additions, yet they are a touch worse with a 3-3-0 mark. Which team might start a hot streak with a W in this one?

Dallas Stars at Colorado Avalanche

8:30 p.m. ET (TNT) | COL -148, O/U: 5.5

It's rare for two teams to play each other on back-to-back nights, and even rarer for two members of the NHL's top echelon to do so. After finishing first and third in the league during the 2025-26 regular season, the Avs and the Stars have not quite gotten out to that type of start this campaign, but both are expected to be right in the mix come playoff time. stories.headline: When can Kimi Antonelli win the F1 title? Earliest date, points needed and remaining races
stories.summary: Kimi Antonelli took another big step towards his first world title after outscoring his two closest championship rivals, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, at the Singapore Grand Prix.
stories.body:
Kimi Antonelli took another big step towards his first world title after outscoring his two closest championship rivals, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, at the Singapore Grand Prix.

The 20-year-old, who has the potential to set a new record for the youngest Formula 1 champion this year, now leads Mercedes teammate Russell by 102 points in the standings with a maximum of 150 points still up for grabs.

The substantial lead means he could be crowned champion as early as Oct. 24 at the U.S. Grand Prix in Austin, but the maths around that calculation are slightly complicated by question marks over the final two races of the season. The grands prix in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are currently scheduled to go ahead on Nov. 29 and Dec. 6, but escalations in the war between the United States and Iran have the potential to force the cancellation of both rounds.

F1 has put a contingency plan in place to hold a single round at Imola if Qatar and Abu Dhabi are cancelled, but doing so would cut the championship short by one round and mean only 125 points are available to any single driver before the end of the year. Such a scenario would change the maths around the championship fight, making it easier for Antonelli to be crowned champion in Austin.

- 'Chucky' Verstappen is back. Luckily for Antonelli and Mercedes, it's too late

- Max Verstappen takes back-to-back wins with dominant drive at Singapore GP

- Lewis Hamilton calls Singapore GP strategy 'painful lesson' after Ferrari apology

Alongside Russell and Hamilton, Max Verstappen, Charles Leclerc and Lando Norris are still mathematically in contention for this year's championship, although the incredibly slim hopes of Leclerc and Norris would be snuffed out entirely by the cancellation of the races in the Middle East.

What does Antonelli need to do to be crowned champion in Austin?
Assuming the final two races go ahead as planned, Antonelli's chances of clinching the title in Austin remain relatively slim. The Mercedes driver would need to win in Texas, with his teammate Russell finishing ninth or lower and Hamilton finishing fifth or lower.

Such a scenario would put Antonelli 125 points ahead of Russell with 125 points remaining, but even if Antonelli failed to score another point and Russell won all the remaining rounds after Austin, Antonelli would still be crowned champion on countback of race victories (by that stage Antonelli would be on nine and Russell on three with five races remaining).

If the championship is shortened by the season ending in Imola rather than Abu Dhabi, Antonelli would only need to leave Austin with a lead of 100 points over his rivals.

Such a scenario would result in the following permutations:

If Antonelli wins in Austin he would be crowned champion regardless of where the others finish.
If Antonelli finishes second, he would be crowned champion if Russell doesn't win the race.
If Antonelli finishes third, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes off the podium.
If Antonelli finishes fourth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes behind him and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes fifth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes fourth or lower and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes sixth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes fifth or lower and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes seventh, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes sixth or lower and Hamilton does not finish in the top two.
If Antonelli finishes eighth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes seventh or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top two and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes ninth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes eighth or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top three and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes tenth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes ninth or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top three and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli fails to score, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes ninth or lower, Hamilton finishes fifth or lower and Verstappen does not win the race.

What's the minimum Antonelli needs to do be crowned champion?
Another way to look at the championship is the minimum amount of points Antonelli needs to score over the remaining rounds to secure the title regardless of what other drivers achieve. Assuming Qatar and Abu Dhabi go ahead, he needs 49 points over the remaining rounds, which could be achieved with as little as five sixth place finishes and one fifth place finish over the rest of the season.

If only five races remain, Antonelli would need just 24 points to secure the title, which would be attainable with two seventh place finishes and three eighth place finishes at the remaining rounds.

stories.headline: The UFC's flyweights are hot again - is Lone'er Kavanagh the next star?
stories.summary: Could a breakout win at UFC 333 propel Britain's Lone'er Kavanagh into the flyweight title picture?
stories.body:
The fighting life of a UFC flyweight was once an unenvied one.

Constant uncertainty over the future of the division, a lack of big pay-per-view interest and an unfortunate routine of far too many fighters getting cut for the weight class to sustain itself were just some of the problems that characterised the modern era. UFC president Dana White put it in simple terms, saying after Demetrious Johnson's UFC exit in 2018 that "people didn't care" about the flyweights. Even Olympic gold medalist and former two-division champion Henry Cejudo struggled to see how the flyweight division would continue as a part of the UFC, with his own brash persona and entertaining title defences pivotal to maintaining awareness of the division.

Much has changed since the days of Cejudo though, and the flyweights now have a genuine claim to being one of the most exciting divisions in the whole of the UFC. And one man at the forefront of that charge is another promising fighting talent from across the Atlantic, with England's Lone'er Kavanagh enjoying a rise like few others this past year.

He accepted a short-notice fight against ex-champion Brandon Moreno in the lion's den of Mexico City in March and produced one of the most stunning UFC upsets in recent memory, taking the unanimous decision win in front of a hostile crowd. Kavanagh was unranked before that fight and despite more recently losing to Brandon Royval at UFC 329, he remains just a win away from breaking into the flyweight title conversation. Taking on Royval on the night of Conor McGregor's return in Las Vegas in July, Kavanagh was submitted but earned the fight of the night on one of the promotion's most-watched recent cards in a back-and-forth slugfest. The 27-year-old's exciting style and high ceiling was on show that evening and will be again when he faces Ramazonbek Temirov on what is remarkably just his second high-profile numbered event at UFC 333 on Oct. 24.

"Thinking back to certain moments [in Mexico City], it was like a rollercoaster, it was a sick opportunity and I'm glad I did it and my team backed me to do it," Kavanagh tells ESPN.

"[Royval was] another step on the journey, losing is never fun, no matter what stage you're at whether you're at the top or at any point of your career but unfortunately sometimes you have to learn like that -- learning on the go, that's what we're doing right now.

"I believe I've got the best team around me so I truly believe with this team I can make it all the way to the top and that's the plan, that's the aim.

"I'm always trying to work on things from every fight. Unfortunately, you learn a lot more when you lose."

For Kavanagh, the lights have quickly turned brighter. Like many of his British counterparts in the UFC, he was made in Cage Warriors, the organisation that can take credit for the likes of McGregor, Paddy Pimblett and Tom Aspinall. From there, a first round knockout on Dana White's Contender Series saw the journey in the big time begin. His first professional defeat came in the UFC against the experienced Charles Johnson, but that was quickly forgotten with the Moreno heist that saw his stock in the game skyrocket. Kavanagh's front-footed, devious style stemming from his kickboxing roots has even earned him praise from one of the greatest to ever step in the octagon with a Jon Jones Facetime after that UFC Mexico win leaving him "starstruck."

"Your Muay Thai is beautiful, your kicks, they don't show at all. They have no telegraph. It's so nice," Jones said to Kavanagh.

It is a style that was born at London's Great Britain Top Team (GBTT), where alongside UFC veteran Nathaniel Wood and fellow prospect Shanelle Dyer, Kavanagh has honed his craft, going from a five-time K1 kickboxing champion to now potentially a statement win away from challenging for UFC gold under British MMA trailblazer Brad Pickett. And that too in a division where the competition is possibly as fierce as it has ever been. Royval, Tatsuro Tairo, Manuel Kape, Asu Almabayev and bona fide flyweight royalty Alexandre Pantoja make up the spine of a group of challengers that Kananagh finds himself a part of.

Joshua Van's UFC 331 title defence ended any doubts about his validity as champion, with a dominant win over Pantoja, and at just 24-years-old he looks set for a stint at the top -- where Kavanagh aspires to be. But first, No. 7 ranked, one below Kavanagh, and unbeaten in the UFC, the explosive Temirov is one of the toughest challenges the Englishman has faced in his career, and in a weight class as deep as the flyweights, back-to-back losses would see Kavanagh fall mercilessly down the pecking order -- the stakes are high at UFC 333.

"I think the flyweight division is the best division at the moment. It's forever changing," Kavanagh says. "There are so many young up and comers but there are also so many people that have been around for so long. So it's got a good mixture of everything and to be honest, just excited to be a part of it - it's sick being a flyweight at this time.

"I'm a very 'one fight at a time' kind of person, I'll always look at what's in front of me and then what's next but I think it would be an exciting fight either way, [Joshua] Van vs. Lon."

Born in London to an Irish father and Chinese mother, Kavanagh wears his heritage on his sleeve with his name Lone'er translating to "Little Dragon" in English. He credits his mum for pushing him into MMA, a decision that has since paid dividends.

Kavanagh is now set to be a part of a main card alongside two title fights at the Etihad Arena in Abu Dhabi. In his way, Uzbekistan's Temirov is coming in red hot on the back of a first-round finish against Steve Erceg, he last tasted defeat in an MMA bout seven years ago and has never been knocked out.

"I haven't seen all the fighters just fighting like me. Just striking punches, just making knockouts. But my punches will just kill them all," Temirov told the UFC.

The kickboxer is aware of the danger that Temirov carries but also the opportunity up for grabs.

"I think a win there puts me right back up there. He's a dangerous opponent. He's got some good wins under him, a lot of wins, but I think a win against him puts me right back up at the top. [I'm] always looking for a finish," Kavanagh said.

"His main weapons are his heavy hands, and that excites me. I love fights like that and I think it's a good fight for me. Hopefully [another fight of the night], I'm looking for more performances of the night."

As is now customary with Kavanagh's UFC bouts, his throwdown against the formidable Temirov is one not to be missed. With the top of the flyweight division so deep he will want to turn all the excitement surrounding him into consistency to earn a shot at Van's belt, that journey will take its latest step in a treacherous division.

And as Bruce Buffer introduces both fighters, perhaps there will be something for the UFC bosses and fans alike to take away before a single punch is even thrown. That all these years after Cejudo and Johnson have been and gone, the flyweights are box office property once again.

stories.headline: Dream's Gray has minor procedure on hand ahead of Finals opener
stories.summary: Allisha Gray, who has missed the Dream's past two playoff games because of a left hand injury, is still day-to-day heading into the WNBA Finals after undergoing a minor procedure.
stories.body:
Four-time All-Star Allisha Gray underwent a minor procedure on her left hand and is still considered day-to-day for the Atlanta Dream heading into the WNBA Finals, she said Tuesday.

"Progress is great," Gray told WSB-TV when asked at practice whether she'd play in Game 1. "As of right now just day-to-day, and you'll see."

Gray did not clarify whether she had surgery on her hand, and the team declined to say when the procedure occurred.

She was seen taking shots at practice Tuesday, a day before the team travels to the Bay Area for Saturday's Finals opener against No. 2 seed Golden State.

Gray, the top scorer for the No. 4 seed Dream, has missed the past two playoff games after injuring the hand in the first half of Game 1 in a semifinal series against the New York Liberty. She was listed as questionable heading into Game 3 last Friday against New York and went through warmups before being ruled out "in the interest of caution," according to coach Karl Smesko.

The Dream advanced to the Finals with a three-game sweep.

Gray, a 6-foot guard out of South Carolina, averaged 19.0 points, 3.5 rebounds, 2.6 assists and 1.4 steals this year while appearing in all 44 regular-season games. She was also the Dream's top scorer (22.0 points per game) during their first-round sweep of the No. 5 seed Washington Mystics.

The Dream and Valkyries will both be competing for their first WNBA championship.

stories.headline: Garber won't dish on exchange with Messi: 'Between me and Leo'
stories.summary: Don Garber has addressed his September confrontation with Lionel Messi, and the MLS commissioner said he admired the exchange.
stories.body:
Don Garber has addressed his confrontation with Lionel Messi following Inter Miami CF Campeones Cup victory over Cruz Azul in September, with the MLS commissioner saying he admired the exchange.

Following the Campeones Cup victory, Messi and Garber could be seen having a heated discussion before the Inter Miami captain went to celebrate the victory with the rest of his team and family members.

"You know, the best players in the world have passion," Garber said in an interview with Front Office Sports on Tuesday. "The legendary players have more than passion. Leo played on Saturday, scored a couple goals and assists coming out of an international window where he played for Argentina, 39 years old. He's leading our rush for Golden Boot. He's leading our MVP race.

"There are players throughout history, Muhammad Ali, Wayne Gretzky, Michael Jordan who play with a sense of intensity and passion that makes them unique and special, and makes him the GOAT of all GOATS. What is going on there is between me and Leo [Messi], it's not something I am going to talk about with you.

"But I admire it, I appreciate it and I think it's what makes Leo Messi the greatest player ever to play football. And I will say, [he's] the greatest athlete of all time."

Inter Miami beat Cruz Azul 2-0 in the Campeones Cup final with a goal from Messi in the 24th minute before he provided the assist to Casemiro for the second goal. Messi currently has 23 goals and 13 assists in MLS, leading the 2026 Golden Boot race and sitting in second place for most assists so far this regular season.

It's not the first time that Garber and Messi haven't seen eye to eye. In 2025, Garber made a joke about Messi not wanting to talk to him following the decision to suspend him and former teammate Jordi Alba for missing the 2025 MLS All-Star Game.

"I don't think he wants to talk to me," Garber said in 2025. "I didn't treat him like any other player in that decision. So, I probably won't be going to Miami any time soon or hanging out and doing any media work with Leo."

Garber later defended his decision to suspend the two players.

"If you don't do that, you're not gonna be able to lead," Garber said. "You're not gonna be able to command the respect of the ownership. The media is going to s--- on you no matter what. You guys will write a story 'how could you suspend Leo Messi?' after we suspended him, and before we suspended him say 'how could you not?'

"So, the media is irrelevant to that equation. They're gonna hate you all the time."

Garber and Messi later interacted at the 2025 MLS Cup, when the MLS commissioner presented the Inter Miami captain with the trophy. Inter Miami currently sits second place on the Eastern Conference table with 49 points from 28 games.

stories.headline: NRL: Spencer Leniu signs with Eels after early Roosters release
stories.summary: Spencer Leniu has signed a four-year deal with Parramatta just days after winning his fourth NRL premiership with the Sydney Roosters.
stories.body:
Spencer Leniu has signed a four-year deal with Parramatta just days after winning his fourth NRL premiership with the Sydney Roosters.

Leniu finished his three-year stint at the Tricolours on a high after a stellar performance in their 19-18 win over Newcastle to secure the 2026 trophy.

The NSW Origin representative added the Roosters' premiership ring to the three he won with Penrith from 2021-2023.

Leniu was granted a release from the final year of his Roosters contract, which will give the club some salary cap reprieve

The hard-hitting forward's Eels contract is reportedly worth more than the $850,000 per year he was making with Easts, where he spent much of his time coming off the bench.

He is expected to play a more active role in blue and gold, leading the line for the Eels' forward pack.

The westward move will see the former Panther reunite with good friend Jarome Luai, but first the pair will both suit up for Toa Samoa at the Rugby League World Cup.

Eels general manager of football Mark O'Neill shared his delight at signing one of the game's "premier enforcers".

"We're thrilled to have Spencer join the Parramatta Eels and become part of what we're building at this club," O'Neill said in a statement.

"He's one of the elite middle forwards in the game and has consistently performed on the biggest stages throughout his career.

The exit of Leniu adds to the exodus of stars from the Roosters premiership lineup.

Angus Crichton and Mark Nawaqanitawase are rugby-bound, Daly Cherry-Evans is joining Hull FC, while Daniel Tupou retired this week after his 307-game career.

Connor Watson, who missed the title decider due to concussion, has signed for a season with St George Illawarra Dragons.

Roosters coach Trent Robinson said Leniu had been a strong contributor during his time at the club.

"Spencer has brought a lot to our group over the last three years, both through the way he plays and the energy and personality he brings every day," Robinson said in a statement on Thursday.

"He brings an intensity and competitiveness to everything he does, and he challenges the people around him to be better.

"To see him finish his time here as a premiership winner is something he should be really proud of, and something we'll always share together."

With his departure announced at the Roosters' awards night on Wednesday, Leniu said he would leave the club on a high.

""I'm proud to have worn the Roosters jersey and I'll always have a lot of love and respect for the club, the boys and everyone who has supported me during my time here," said Leniu.

"Winning a premiership with this group and sharing that with the boys, our families and everyone at the club is something I'll carry with me for the rest of my life."

stories.headline: What this year's MLB playoffs say about baseball's future
stories.summary: The No. 1 payroll in baseball -- and three others that barely add up to L.A.'s combined -- are left standing this October.
stories.body:
MILWAUKEE -- Something very confusing is happening in Major League Baseball. For much of the 2026 season, the league has run a public campaign that paints the game as fundamentally broken, unfair for lower-payroll and smaller-market teams, remedied only by a salary cap and floor system it says would fix such imbalances. Meanwhile, of the four teams remaining in the postseason, one plays in the game's smallest market, another is carrying the game's lowest cash payroll and a third is running out the 26th-highest payroll of the league's 30 teams.

The fourth team, of course, is the Los Angeles Dodgers, the behemoth whose back-to-back championships have underpinned MLB's rhetoric about the game's future upon the expiration of the collective bargaining agreement Dec. 1. The league regularly cites the Dodgers in its polemics on payroll; L.A.'s this year is $340.6 million with an additional $180.8 million in luxury tax payments, according to Ethan Hulihen's payroll tracker. The penalty Los Angeles will pay this season is greater than the full payrolls of the other three championship series clubs, the Milwaukee Brewers ($143.7 million), Tampa Bay Rays ($98.5 million) and Cleveland Guardians ($74.4 million). On cash payroll alone, the Dodgers are outspending the Brewers, Rays and Guardians combined by nearly $25 million.

And yet with the Dodgers losing the first two games of the National League Championship Series, MLB is looking at a reality that directly opposes its narrative: two small market teams in the World Series. And not just any small markets, either: Tampa Bay hasn't won a title in its 29 years of existence, Milwaukee hasn't won a title in its 58 years of existence and Cleveland hasn't won a title since 1948. This October could very easily deliver the sort of World Series that fulfills the desire of commissioner Rob Manfred, who during the All-Star break told reporters that "competitive balance" is "the core of what we're about."

While 2026 doesn't necessarily invalidate MLB's argument -- that moneyed teams over the past decade have dominated the postseason landscape, and any single season that suggests otherwise is an outlier -- it absolutely validates the MLB Players Association's contention that the game's financial landscape doesn't disqualify lower-spending teams from success and does not necessitate a cap-and-floor system. If Milwaukee captures the NL pennant, the combined payrolls of the two World Series team would be the lowest since the St. Louis Cardinals beat the Texas Rangers in 2011.

Even so, owners do not intend to pivot from their contentions. Their insistence on a cap and floor -- backed, the league says, by surveys that show fans want one -- remains firm no matter who wins the Fall Classic, according to sources. Accordingly, collective bargaining talks have been at a standstill since the league in May proposed a 50/50 revenue split with a $245.3 million ceiling and $171.2 million floor. Not only is the union viscerally opposed to a cap, but it also contends players would lose hundreds of millions of dollars in such a system.

Upon delivering the parameters of one to the MLBPA in May, the league said in a statement that "the biggest issue ... is fixing the payroll disparity" and that "too many fans in too many markets have too little hope their team has a fair chance to win."

The players remaining in the postseason have a different story to tell.

FOR THE FIRST six years of his career, Jake Bauers lived the nomadic existence of a player on the fringes. It took him from Tampa Bay to Cleveland to Seattle to New York and, finally, to Milwaukee, where he is now the cleanup hitter for the team that won a major league-best 103 regular-season games.

Bauers' travels have given him a unique perspective on the 2026 season. And he doesn't believe it's an accident that the Rays, Guardians and Brewers are among baseball's final four. Since 2016, they have combined for 22 playoff appearances, eight league championship series berths and two World Series attempts, neither successful. All three are regarded by their peers as model organizations, not just for their ability to win consistently on a tight budget but the style of play they embrace and embody.

"You can't just throw nine guys out there and say, play fundamental baseball and expect to win," Bauers said. "There still has to be a certain amount of talent in the room. And I think if you get the right guys who will buy into what you're preaching, who are also talented, who can hit a homer in a big spot when you need them to, but who can also hit a backside ground ball when you need them to, get a bunt down, play good enough defense and base run well -- that, to me, is what every team left has in common."

The commonalities of the three small-market survivors -- they extend to the Dodgers, too -- are clear with a dive into the numbers. The four teams left all do important things well. Each boasts a strong bullpen. Milwaukee and Tampa Bay rank first and second, respectively, in batting average, and the Brewers also lead MLB in walk rate and on-base percentage. The Rays strike out less than any team in MLB -- with Cleveland not far behind in fifth, and its walk rate is eighth. All three are demons on the basepaths, as Tampa Bay ranks second, Milwaukee fifth and Cleveland seventh in stolen bases. As gauche as the sacrifice bunt has become, the small-market mavens embrace its utility and believe a willingness to use it fosters selflessness -- and with the Rays leading MLB in sacrifices, the Brewers fifth and the Guardians eighth, they practice what they preach.

"Anybody on our team can get the bunt sign and put it down," Brewers All-Star second baseman Brice Turang said, and he illustrated that in Game 1 of the NLCS. With Milwaukee trailing the Dodgers 1-0, Turang somehow powered a low and in sinker from left-hander Tarik Skubal to the opposite field for a solo home run. Two plate appearances later, with Milwaukee clinging to a 2-1 advantage, Turang stepped into the batter's box following a leadoff single from Jackson Chourio. On the first pitch, he laid down a perfect sacrifice bunt.

"That's all I've ever known baseball to be," Turang said. "Being able to bunt guys over, move them over. The situation of the game called me to bunt and move them over. And that's what I'm trying to do. I'm trying to help the team win in any way I can. So if that's a bunt, a stolen base or whatever, just trying to do that."

This is not to suggest that small-market teams can bunt their way to the World Series. It's more of a mentality that can speak to lower-payroll clubs: If there are inherent financial disadvantages -- and in a capped system, there still would be, though not nearly as distinct -- teams need to forge an identity that can bridge the gap.

"There's no formula to it, and I know this being a kind of guy who doesn't match the idea of slug, homers, all that kind of stuff," said outfielder Stephen Kwan, the second-longest tenured Guardians player behind star third baseman Jose Ramirez. "I think that's a sign that if you play really good baseball, you do the fundamentals, you do the right thing, you can win any kind of baseball game anytime."

Each player queried on the matter mentioned fundamentals, and that goes for the teams' defense as well. The Rays were the earliest adopters of accepting a lesser bat for superior defense. Tampa Bay also has been the industry standard in strike throwing, while the Guardians and Brewers have turned into pitching development machines. Cleveland's ability to develop top-tier starting pitching dates two decades and today includes left-hander Parker Messick and American League Championship Series Game 3 starter Gavin Williams. The Brewers' history goes back about a decade and today has produced Jacob Misiorowski, Logan Henderson and a bevy of other arms.

At the end of the day, all three of the low-payroll teams left recognize just how random the MLB postseason is -- and how regardless of their regular-season successes, they could've just as easily lost in the division series. Milwaukee needed to play a near-perfect series -- and get some luck -- to oust the San Diego Padres. If Aaron Judge is healthy, perhaps the New York Yankees would've pushed Tampa Bay. And Cleveland needed to win three consecutive games, including a capper on the road, to dispatch a plucky Chicago White Sox club.

"There's not one recipe to have a winning team," said Messick, an All-Star this year and likely finalist for AL Rookie of the Year. "I think we are living proof of that."

OVER THE PAST decade, payroll disparity in MLB has grown significantly. The Dodgers, with the largest local TV deal in the game -- and, due to a bankruptcy court settlement, sharing a fraction of their revenue compared to other teams -- in 2026 are spending at least twice as much as 26 clubs, three times as much as 15, four times as much as 11 and five times as much as seven.

At the All-Star Game, when addressing the nearly $450 million chasm between the top and bottom, Manfred said: "It defies human experience to ask a fan to think that the bottom end of that gap has the same opportunity to win as the top."

Well, the Guardians are at the bottom end of that gap. And after splitting the first two games of the ALCS at Tropicana Field, they seemingly have a better opportunity to win, at least in 2016.

"There's not a competition issue. There's truly not," said Guardians first baseman Nathaniel Lowe, who came up in the Rays organization and has played in markets big (Boston and Texas) and small (Cincinnati). "If owners wanted to spend, they would, and teams that might not spend the money on a roster still find a way to win. So look at the four. It's not a payroll issue. It's commitment to winning. And now being on this side of it, having spent time in Tampa, the payroll isn't really the issue. It's just the commitment to winning."

How one quantifies a commitment to winning is the trouble. Payroll is an easy vector, and the numbers MLB cites -- even this year, eight of the top 10 spending teams qualified for the postseason -- have merit. Teams from bottom-10 markets -- Tampa is 19th, Cleveland 25th and Milwaukee 30th, for context -- have comprised less than a quarter of LCS qualifiers dating more than a quarter-century. The last bottom-10 market team to make the World Series was Cleveland in 2016, following back-to-back appearances from the Kansas City Royals, who was the last one to win in 2015.

"The data in our sport is stark," Manfred said. "Your opportunity to make the playoffs if you are a larger-market team is dramatically higher and your opportunity to proceed to the subsequent rounds -- that advantage grows with each round."

Not in 2026. Whether it's anomalous or the beginning of the best-run organizations regularly making deep playoff runs is for the future to tell. But the Rays, Guardians and Brewers all answer the most important questions for teams with financial disadvantages. Where can they improve? What is their identity? As sick as fans in Pittsburgh and Cincinnati and Baltimore and Miami are of the feeling that larger payrolls are an insurmountable hurdle, players, by and large, don't concern themselves with such matters. It's out of their control.

What's within the control of these franchises? In Milwaukee, for example, taking advantage of the money the organization has funneled toward infrastructure, such as building the largest international scouting staff in the game. Or buying into the Rays way of doing things, with the knowledge that no team has done a better job over the long haul of taking players who struggled elsewhere and finding the best in them. Or recognizing the value of stability in Cleveland, where Chris Antonetti has been running baseball operations longer than anyone outside of Brian Cashman with the Yankees.

Nobody knows how long baseball will shutter when the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 1. Discussions could remain at a standstill. The parties could wind up in court. Or on Capitol Hill, meeting with Congress, trying to reach some sort of détente to save the season. It's also eminently possible that Opening Day comes and goes and fans suffer for the mother of all self-inflicted wounds by those in charge of the game.

What's undeniable is that right now, in the year that MLB staked its argument for a cap around the inability to teams with less than to reasonably compete, 75% of the teams left in the postseason -- and at least 50% of those in the World Series -- are more than reasonably competing. They harbor championship dreams, and they don't believe they're where they are by accident.

"There is a right way to play the game of baseball, and if you can commit to that and get an entire team to commit to that, you can overcome a lot of things," Bauers said. "As far as payrolls and all that, you've still got to play the game. And all the talent and all the money in the world can't buy the focus that you need to win baseball games."
